| PC_NOT_SHARED or PC_RECOMPILE | Local scope changes to the modules, program, or interface.                             | The PC_NOT_SHARED or PC_RECOMPILE messages are issued for partitions that need to be recompiled and the message points to the module line that is subjected to recompilation. Recompiling DUT from the ./central_dir/dut_ top shared library and the ./central_dir/test test file. | Warning-[PC_NOT_SHARED] Cannot reuse shared partition Cannot reuse partition 'dut_top' from shared library './common_dir'Modified Design Units :                  |
| PC_SKIP_FULLDR                | Local scope change to the internal modules and no change in the global view of design. | The PC_SKIP_FULLDR message is issued.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              | Note-[PC_SKIP_FULLDR] Skipping partcomp design resolutionSkipping partition compile global design resolution as there was no change in the global view of design. |

## Note:

If you use the -q option during compilation:

- In scratch compile, the PC\_GEN\_PARTITION message is suppressed.
- In incremental compile, the PC\_RECOMPILE message is suppressed.

## Partition Compile Use Model

Partition Compile can be used with VCS Two-step Flow or Three-step Flow.

## The Partition Compile Two-Step Flow

1. Synopsys recommends using autopartitioning using the -partcomp option. This is the default mode in partition compile flow. For more details, see the Autopartitioning section.
2. You can create a partition configuration file to generate different partitions than autopartitioning to fine-tune the performance. This is not mandatory step and can be chosen only when you are looking for different partitioning.

<!-- image -->

For an elementary design that has a module named mod in a Verilog library named MYLIB (filename mod.v ) and another module named tb (filename tb.v ). To create a partition for each module definition, the configuration file is in Example 54.

## Example 54 Configuration File for Partition Compile

```
// configuration file config.txt partition cell MYLIB.mod; partition cell tb;
```

In Example 54 one partition is for all instances of module mod and another partition is for all instances of module tb .

You can specify different partitions for different instances (see Cell or Instance Based Partitions ).

For V2K or SV packages (see The Partition Compile Three Step Flow).

You can also use a V2K or SV configuration to specify partitions instead of using an +optconfigfile configuration (see Instance or Cell Based Partitions in a V2K/SV Configuration).

- In addition to the partitions you specify, VCS creates internal or default partitions for the following parts of the design:

a partition for the top-level module

a partition for all SystemVerilog packages

a partition for all SystemVerilog interfaces

1. Run the simulation.

```
% simv
```

There is no runtime option for Partition Compile.

- a. Based on the simulation results, modify the source code. Let's say you only modify tb.v .
- b. Re-compile the design as follows for Partition Compile again by entering the same exact compilation command line:

```
% vi tb.v
```

```
% vcs tb.v -y MYLIB +libext+.v -partcomp
```

For user-defined partitions, re-compile the design as follows:

```
% vcs tb.v -y MYLIB +libext+.v -partcomp \ +optconfigfile+config.txt
```

## 2. Run the simulation again.

```
% simv
```

## The Partition Compile Three Step Flow

Partition Compile supports the three step flow too (analysis, elaboration, and simulation).

Here are the steps to run the Partition Compile in the three step flow:

## Analysis of Code

- Analyze the files using the regular VCS commands. There is no extra option needed at the analysis stage for Partition Compile.
- Verilog/SV designs and testbenches use the vlogan command.
- VHDL designs and test benches use the vhdlan command. For more information see Specifying Partitions in a VHDL Configuration File.
- Mixed HDL designs and testbenches use the vlogan and vhdlan commands.

Here is the synopsys\_sim.setup file for example Example 55:

## Example 55 synopsys\_sim.setup File

```
WORK > DEFAULT DEFAULT : ./rtllib rtllib : ./rtllib
```

The example vlogan command line to analyze the source code in Example 53 is as follows

```
% vlogan -work rtllib -sverilog test.v add_mult.v top.v \ [other options]
```

After analyzing the files, the next step is elaboration. The example vcs command to compile the design in the Partition Compile flow is as follows:

```
% vcs -partcomp top [other options]
```

To specify additional partitions, use the +optconfigfile option as follows:

```
% vcs -partcomp top +optconfigfile+cfg.txt [other options]
```

For more details, refer to Step 2 of Two-Step flow.

## Commonly Used Partition-Compile Options

You can use the following options for partition compile flow:

```
-dir=< _name> -dir/-partcomp_dir=<dir_name>
```

<!-- image -->

Generates partition information in the specified directory.

```
-sharedlib -sharedlib/-partcomp_sharedlib=<dir_name>
```

Reuses the existing partition information from the specified partition database and recompiles only the modified design-specific partitions.

## Limiting Partitions

You can use the following options to limit the module and package partitions in partition compile flow:

```
-partcomp=modpart_limit:N
```

Limits the module partitions to the specified number.

```
-partcomp=pkgpart_limit:N
```

Limits the package partitions to the specified number.

## Note:

The modpart\_limit and pkgpart\_limit are considered as guidelines by the VCS partitioner. The tool can still create slightly more or slightly less partitions based on the module or package sizes and inter-dependencies.

## Specifying a Location for the Partition Data Generation

Use the -partcom \_di = h -partcomp\_dir=dir\_path option to specify a directory for the partition data, for example:

```
% vcs -partcomp top.v test.v add_mult.v \ -partcomp_dir=./PARTCOMP [other options]
```

Using this example, VCS creates a directory named PARTCOMP to contain the partition data.

For mixed HDL or VHDL designs, a directory named vhdl\_objs ir vhdl\_objs\_dir is created for data related to VHDL partitions. This directory is located in the current path by default. The -partcomp\_dir option changes the location of the vhdl\_objs\_dir to the directory specified by -partcomp\_dir .

## Relocation Methods with Partition Compile

VCS allows you to move the simulation executable to the location of your choice. With the relocated database, you can get the benefit of a faster compile turnaround time by reusing the existing partitions and compiling (relocatable compilation) or running the simulation (relocatable simulation) in a new directory.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

The following are the two methods to relocate the database in partition compile - turbo compile flow:

- Using -simcopy Compile Time Options
- Using simcopy Utility
- Turbo Compile Example

## Using -simcopy Compile Time Options

When the -simcopy compile-time options are used along with -partcomp\_sharedlib , it enables VCS TurboCompile flow (by reusing existing partitions) and also enables relocatable compilation or relocatable simulation in a new directory. It helps to run the simulation in parallel for multiple user environments.

## Note:

It is not recommended to use the -kdb=only and -kdb=postelab options along with the VCS -simcopy option.

The -simcopy options are listed in the following table:

Table 18 The -simcopy Compile Time Options

| Option   |                 | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   | Use Model                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|----------|-----------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| -simcopy | ( default mode) | This option moves the partitions from the partition library (default: partitionlib unless specified with -partcomp_dir ) into the simv.daidir/partitionlib directory.In the subsequent compile step with -partcomp_sharedlib option is used, this option does not copy all partitions, only the partitions shared from the partition library which is specified with -partcomp_sharedlib are copied into the simv.daidir/partitionlib directory in your current working area. | % vcs -partcomp -simcopy The above command moves the partition library, partitionlib directory into the simv.daidir directory and ensures that the complete content is relocatable. Also, enables this directory to be used in the relocatable compilation.Now, you can use the unix copy (cp) command to relocate the simv* folders and run the simulation from the destination directory. % cp -r simv simv.daidir The above command copies the simv.daidir directory to the specified destination directoryIf you run incremental compile in the destination directory, you must remove the simulation database using the following commands: % rm -rf simv* Note : If you add the -simcopy option to an incremental compilation (that is not present in the scratch compilation), it causes recompilation. |

Table 18 The -simcopy Compile Time Options (Continued)

| Option           | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       | Use Model                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
|------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| -simcopy_opts=mv | This option moves partitionlib located in the simv.daidir directory to the specified destination directory. Therefore, saves disk space and compilation time.Note: If the -partcomp_sharedlib is specified, the partitions that are reused are also copied to simv.daidir/partitionlib directory. However, when -simcopy_opts=mv is specified, then the partitions reused from the sharedlib are moved from the original sharedlib to the simv.daidir/partitionlib directory. This makes the original -partcomp_sharedlib unusable. Hence, you must use the -simcopy_opts=mv option with caution. | % vcs <options> -partcomp -simcopy -simcopy_opts=mv You can also use the -simcopy option to enable relocatable compilation. Consider the following example: % vcs -partcomp -simcopy . The above compile command moves the content of partitionlib with three partitions P1, P2, and P3 into simv.daidir/partitionlib at the end of compile. Here, the simcopy_opts=mv option does not affect the scratch compile. % cp -r simv.daidir/partitionlib <destination dir/scratch_partitionlib> The above command copy partitionlib with three partitions P1, P2, and P3 into the specified destination directory. % cd destination dir% \rm -rf simv* csrc*% vcs -partcomp -simcopy -simcopy_opts=mv -partcomp_sharedlib= <scratch_partitionlib> The above commands apply incremental compilation to the sharedlib. Considering that the partitions P1 and P2 are reused and P3 is recompiled, the partitionlib directory has only one partition P3. So, in this case -simcopy_opt=mv option ensures that the partitions P1 and P2 are moved from scratch_partitionlib to simv.dairdir/partitionlib. |

## Using simcopy Utility

VCS provides the simcopy utility that is available inside the simv.daidir directory to relocate databases after the compilation. Multiple users can use this utility as it supports relocatable compilation and relocatable simulation which can also be done in parallel.

Following is the use model:

1. Use the following command to generate partitionlib : % vcs &lt;options&gt; -partcomp Note : The partitionlib directory need to be retained to get the coverage score, when the partition compile is used in the flow. Otherwise, URG or Verdi shows empty coverage data.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

2. The following command moves partitionlib to simv.daidir and creates a copy of simv at the specified destination directory. The original simv is not deleted.

```
% simv.daidir/simcopy <destination dir> Note: The simcopy utility also has simv.daidir/simcopy -inline option which
```

runs simcopy utility in inline mode.

You must follow below mentioned guidelines when you use the simcopy utility:

- After you copy the database using the simcopy utility, you must point to the partitionlib inside the simv.daidir directory and not to your current directory.
- If you are updating the sharedlib area, you should first clean the existing sharedlib and then copy the new partitionlib to avoid overwriting.

## Turbo Compile Example

This section describes turbo compile flow with the use case of -partcomp\_sharedlib and -simcopy options.

In this use case,

- Compiling source (RTL and test) files in different directories and the source is changed during recompile.

Consider the following use case:

Table 19 rtl.v and test.v

| %cat ./src/rtl.v                                                                                                                                                | %cat ./src/test.v                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| module rtl_count(input reg clk,rst, output reg [3:0] cnt); always@(posedge clk or posedge rst) begin if(rst) cnt <= 4'b0000; else cnt <= cnt + 1; end endmodule | module top; reg clk,rst; reg [3:0] cnt; always #5 clk = ~ clk; rtl_count inst (clk,rst,cnt); initial $monitor($time," clk = %b rst = %b cnt = %0d",clk,rst,cnt); initial begin rst = 1'b1; clk= 1'b0; #100 $finish; end endmodule |

Run the design using the following commands:

```
% rm -rf simv* csrc* partition* *dir* % vlogan -sverilog ./src/rtl.v ./src/test.v % vcs -sverilog -partcomp -simcopy top % cp -r simv.daidir/partitionlib ./some/user/path/last_pc_db % cd ./some/user/path/
```

The above example shows the scratch compile command. After successful compile, copy the partitionlib generated inside simv.daidir to the incremental compile location.

VCS generates the following messages at the scratch compile step that shows the partitions generated with the PC\_GEN\_PARTITION message.

```
Note-[PC_GEN_PARTITION] Generating partition Generating new partition '_vcs_pc_package_' at './partitionlib/_vcs_pc_package__BOvusd'. Note-[PC_GEN_PARTITION] Generating partition Generating new partition 'top' at './partitionlib/top_1YNkOc'.
```

The source file is changed as shown in the following table.

```
Table 2 rtl.v and test.v
```

<!-- image -->

Table 20 rtl.v and test.v

| %cat ./src/rtl.v                                                                                                                                                | %cat ./src/test.v                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| module rtl_count(input reg clk,rst, output reg [3:0] cnt); always@(posedge clk or posedge rst) begin if(rst) cnt <= 4'b0000; else cnt <= cnt + 1; end endmodule | module top; reg clk,rst; reg [3:0] cnt; always #5 clk = ~ clk; rtl_count inst (clk,rst,cnt); initial $monitor($time," clk = %b rst = %b cnt = %0d",clk,rst,cnt); initial begin rst = 1'b1; clk= 1'b0; #3; `ifdef RUN_COUNTER rst = 1'b0; `endif #100 $finish; end endmodule |

## Run the design using the following commands:

```
% vlogan -sverilog ./src/rtl.v ./src/test.v +define+RUN_COUNTER % vcs top -sverilog -partcomp -simcopy -partcomp_sharedlib=last_pc_db % simv
```

During recompilation, use the -partcomp\_sharedlib option that reuses the existing partitions copied from the scratch compile and regenerates only the changed partitions.

VCS generates the following messages at the recompile step that shows the partitions that are newly generated with the PC\_GEN\_PARTITION message and the partitions that are reused with the PC\_SHARED message.

```
Note-[PC_SHARED] Reusing shared partition Reusing partition '_vcs_pc_package_' from shared library 'last_pc_db'. Warning-[PC_NOT_SHARED] Cannot reuse shared partition Cannot reuse partition 'top' from shared library 'last_pc_db' Modified Design Units : top : "./src/test.v", 1
```

<!-- image -->

```
Note-[PC_GEN_PARTITION] Generating partition Generating new partition 'top' at './partitionlib/top_3dviq'.
```

## Note:

VCS generates an error for the following use cases:

- Compiling source files in same directories with same partition directory -partcomp\_dir and -partcomp\_sharedlib directory names during scratch or incremental compilation.
- If -simcopy options are not used consistently at all compile commands, then the relocatable compilation fails.

## Cross-Module References (XMRs)

When your design is partitioned there is a chance that there are cross module references (XMRs) across partitions; that is, signals and variables from one partition being accessed from another partition. You can handle XMRs as follows when using the Partition Compile flow:

- If XMRs are not changing, no extra option or configuration file is needed.
- If XMRs change, both the referrer and the referee partitions are recompiled.
- If XMRs change, you can optimize the compile behavior as follows:
- Any change in XMRs, trigger recompilation of the referee partition.
- Use the -partcom =genX -partcomp=gen\_xmr\_config=top\_module option to generate configuration file that contains the XMR information of the design.
- Pass this configuration file to see optimized recompile behavior where only referred partitions are recompiled. Use the following syntax for the configuration file:
- If you do not specify any option, your design is till compiled or recompiled.

```
xmr {module_or_program_name} {signal_name};
```

This section discusses the following topics:

- Support for Skipping Intra Position Rewrite in Partition Compile Flow
- Usage
- Examples
- Limitation

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## Support for Skipping Intra Position Rewrite in Partition Compile Flow

VCS skips XMR rewrite for intra partition XMR during child compilation.

In the following scenarios, the intra partition XMR cannot be skipped:

- XMR to interface
- XMR target is structure or structure member
- XMR is upward
- XMR target is also the target of cross partition XMR

## Usage

This feature is enabled using the MHID PC\_SKIP\_XMR\_REWRITE .

## Examples

The following are the examples of this feature:

## Example 56 test1.sv

```
module top; sub s(); initial $display(s.a); endmodule module sub; int a; endmodule
```

| Partition Compile Flow With MHID PC_SKIP_XMR_REWRITE                                          | Default Partition Compile Flow                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| pre_rewrite_rad.v: /* M#0 */ module top; sub_7saKSd s(); initial $display(top.s.a); endmodule | pre_rewrite_rad.v: /* M#0 */ module top; int_vcs_pc____vcs_0_a_00000D; sub_7saKSd s(); initial $display(_vcs_pc____vcs_0_a_00000D); initial begin $$xmr_map_rel(0, _vcs_pc____vcs_0_a_00000D, "top.s.a", -2147483648); end endmodule |

## Example 57 test2.sv

```
module top; sub s(); mid m(s.w); endmodule module sub; wire w; endmodule module mid(w); input w; leaf l(w); endmodule module leaf(w); input w; endmodule
```

| Partition Compile Flow With MHID PC_SKIP_XMR_REWRITE                                     | Default Partition Compile Flow                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| pre_rewrite_rad.v: /* M#0 */ module top; sub_7saKSd s(); mid_7saKSd m(top.s.w) endmodule | pre_rewrite_rad.v: /* M#0 */ module top; wire_vcs_pc____vcs_0_w_00000D; sub_7saKSd s(); mid_7saKSd m(_vcs_pc____vcs_0_w_00000D); initial begin $$xmr_map_rel(0, _vcs_pc____vcs_0_w_00000D, "top.s.w", -2147483648); end endmodule |

## Limitation

- Fine-Grained Parallelism (FGP) is not supported for this feature.

## Coding Guidelines

Here are some guidelines  to follow when using the partition compile flow to get the best turnaround time:

- 1.1 Wrap testbench code in SV packages.
- Avoid code in $unit (code changes in the $unit scope triggers recompilation of the entire design).
- Multiple packages can be used to make logical partitions of the code.

<!-- image -->

- 1.2 Avoid XMRs in the testbench code where possible.
- Use SV virtual interfaces.
- XMRs prevent putting code in packages (this is an SV LRM restriction).
- Runtime impact with partition compile (resolutions at runtime).
- Test to test compile time can be high if a large portion of testbench is compiled with each test due to $unit and the testbench contains XMRs to the design.
- If XMRs are required only for debugging purpose, use `ifdef to include the XMR for compilation.
- 1.3 Import packages only where required.
- Package changes can cause recompile of multiple partitions (if all packages are imported in a file and that file is included in many partitions).
- 1.4 Do not assume any specific initial blocks order of execution.
- 1.5 Do not combine source code from multiple partitions in the same file.
- Changes in one partition can cause recompilation of other partitions in the same file.
- Limit optimization in vlogan.
- 1.6 Scripts (Makefile) should not have options that translate to +define+ on the vlogan command line for the testbench or DUT, especially for multiple tests.
- Ensure that test to test does not have to recompile the testbench or DUT. Test specific code should be limited to a test case file.
- Different modes (for example speed) can be configured through variables instead of `define .
- 1.7 Use multiple vlogan commands.
- Logical vlogan commands are:
- 1 for each package
- 1 for test cases
- 1 or more for DUT
- Optimize time for reanalysis.
- Reanalysis of source code (vlogan or vhdlan) with different command-line options causes the recompilation of the source code and all partitions that share the logical library.

<!-- image -->

- $unit changes are local.
- Makefile targets should analyze only required set of files.
- 1.8 For parallel compilation of test cases, preferably have one directory for one test case.
- The test cases should be setup in such a way that multiple test cases can be compiled in parallel and do not over-write the compiled data of other test cases.
- 1.9 If the same file (especially with interfaces and packages) is included in multiple files, the vlogan commands of those multiple files should not direct the analyzed data to different logical libraries.
- 1.10 Interface definition to be passed before the virtual interface is created to the vlogan command.
- Prevents creation of one extra dummy interface partition.
- 1.11 Makefile should not clean by default.

By default, VCS allows calling non-blocking tasks such as tasks without delay, event control or wait statements, from within a function. For blocking task calls, an error message is issued.

In the partition compile flow, the blocking and non-blocking nature of a task call may not always be determined at compile-time. Compilation may complete without errors when calling a blocking task from within a function.

You can use the -partcomp=LRM\_1800\_2012 compile-time option to enable checking of stricter SystemVerilog compliant rule. When the option is specified, an error message is issued in the partition compile flow for calling any tasks, blocking or non-blocking, from within a function.

## Scenarios Causing a Recompilation of a Partition

The following cases cause a recompilation of a partition:

- Change of a module definition in a partition, either instance- or cell-based.
- Change in VCS command-line option (addition, deletion, or sub-argument value change).
- Change in the synopsys\_sim.setup or +optc nfig le +optconfigfile file.
- Global design property changes like adding $dumpvars $dumpvars to a partition, in which case all partitions need to be recompiled.
- Changes to the ports or parameters that affect the ports of a partition. If there is a parent and child partition, and this change is only to the child partition, the parent need not be recompiled.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

- Changes to $unit $unit scope. Any change (addition of a new signal, type, module, or interface) to a $unit causes recompilation of all the partitions associated with the $unit .
- Changes to an interface require the recompilation of all modules connected to that interface.
- Changes to a shared package. In this case, all the partitions sharing this package require recompilation.
- Reanalysis of source code ( vlogan or vhdlan ) with different command-line options causes recompilation of the source code and all partitions that share the logical library.
- Changes in input files like assert hier file, -cm\_hier file, UPF file, and XPROP configuration files.
- The change in a package partition leads to recompilation of its dependent partitions.
- When two or more modules/packages/interfaces are grouped into one partition, then even if only one module/package/interface is changed, the whole partition is recompiled.

## Achieving the Best Turnaround Time with Partition Compile

To get the maximum gain in turnaround time from the partition compile flow, note the following:

- Do not create too many partitions
- Start with autopartitioning and then tune for performance, if needed.
- Avoid code in $unit
- Code changes in the $unit may affect many partitions.
- $unit is not sharable across multiple tests.
- Create separate partitions for each top-level design in hierarchy, if more than one toplevel change in subsequent compilation.
- All parallel top-level are a single partitions, by default.
- Create a separate partition for the top-level that changes frequently compared to the other parallel top-level that are idle.
- Create separate partitions for each test (program) and only test partition gets recompiled in this case.
- Make external IP/VIP modules as separate partitions.

- Partitions for mixed HDL designs
- Create separate partition for a VHDL entity if it is going to change frequently.
- If it is not a separate partition then it is compiled as part of default VHDL top partition.
- Create one or more partitions for SV packages that are going to change frequently.
- Import packages only where required.
- Package changes can cause recompile of multiple partitions (if all packages are imported in a file and that file is included in many partitions).

## Profiling of Compilation Time

The -pcmakeprof compile-time option enables profiling of time spent in each step of a compilation. The profiling result is tabulated and printed at the end of the compilation log. The following are usage examples of the option in different compilation flows:

Single Compile, Two-step

```
vcs -sverilog -pcmakeprof test.sv Single Compile, Three-step vlogan -sverilog test.sv vcs top -pcmakeprof Partition Compile, Two-step vcs -sverilog -partcomp -partcomp_dir=p_dir -pcmakeprof test.sv Partition Compile, Three-step vlogan -sverilog test.sv vcs top -partcomp -partcomp_dir=p_dir -pcmakeprof The following are examples of the profiling result:
```

Single Compile, Two-step Parsing Shows the amount of time consumed by parsing all design files.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

| Partition Compile, Two-step   |
|-------------------------------|

Global\_analysis

Shows the amount of time consumed by loading an analyzed design, resolving the design and creating partitions.

Partition

Shows the amount of time consumed by compiling a particular partition.

Stitching\_&amp;\_Elaboration

Shows the amount of time consumed by stitching all partitions together.

All\_partition\_time

Shows the amount of time consumed by all partitions and stitching the partitions. This number is the sum of the ' Partition ' numbers and the ' Stitching\_&amp;\_Elaboration ' number.

```
Total_time
```

Shows the total amount of time consumed by an entire compilation. This number is the sum of all the ' Activity ' numbers.

## Note:

Due to floating number precision, the value of ' All\_partition\_time ' and ' Total\_time ' may differ slightly from the exact sum of numbers.

## Improving Partition Compile Performance for SDF Designs

In case of SDF interconnect delays, both the source and destination of the interconnect delays are in same partition and therefore DUT is not broken into several partitions. To break the DUT into multiple partitions, support for manual partitions for designs that have SDF interconnect delays across partitions has been added. This allows you to specify explicit partitions to the DUT to achieve better turnaround time.

- Use Model
- Usage Example
- Limitations

## Use Model

To enable this feature, use the -hsopt= im df c -hsopt=hsimsdfic compile-time option.

In case of uphierarchy interconnect delays, use the -hsopt=uphierarchyic switch.

## Usage Example

Consider the following examples:

## Example 58 basic.v

```
`timescale 1ns/1ns /// ------------ Top level ASIC modules----------------// //*** top level asic dut_1*** module dut_1 (clk,in,out); input clk; inout  in; inout out; buf (out, in); endmodule //*** top level asic dut_2 *** module dut_2 (clk,in,out); input clk; inout in; inout out; not (out, in);
```

<!-- image -->

```
endmodule endmodule basic_cfg // separating asic_top and sdf loader partition instance tb.asic_top; partition instance tb.sdf_loader; // separating top level asic modules partition instance tb.asic_top.dut_1_inst_1; partition instance tb.asic_top.dut_2_inst_1;
```

<!-- image -->

```
/// ------------ System Modules : Interconnect top level ASIC modules ---------// module top(inout in1,inout in2,inout out1,inout out2,input clk); dut_1 dut_1_inst_1(clk,in1,out1); dut_2 dut_2_inst_1(clk,in2,out2); endmodule //-------------- Testbench Module : Stimulus generation ------------// module tb(); wire  in_1,in_2; wire out_dut_1,out_dut_2; reg  rin1,rin2; assign in_1 = rin1; assign in_2 = rin2; reg clk=0; always #20  clk = !clk; top asic_top(in_1,in_2,out_dut_1,out_dut_2,clk); sdf_loader sdf_loader(); initial begin #21  rin1 = 1; #80  rin1 = 0; #80  rin1 = 1; #80  rin1 = 0; #100; #40  rin2 = 1; #80  rin2 = 0; #80  rin2 = 1; #80  rin2 = 0; #100; $finish(); end endmodule //-------------------------- SDF LOADER -----------------------// module sdf_loader(); initial begin $sdf_annotate("basic_top.sdf", tb.asic_top); end
```

## Example 59

## Example 60 basic\_top.sdf

<!-- image -->

```
(DELAYFILE (SDFVERSION "OVI 3.0") (DIVIDER .) (TIMESCALE 1ns) (CELL (CELLTYPE "top" ) (INSTANCE ) (DELAY (ABSOLUTE ( INTERCONNECT  in1   dut_1_inst_1.in   (1)(4) ) ( INTERCONNECT  in2   dut_2_inst_1.in   (2)(3) ) ) ) ) )
```

## You can use the following command to run the example:

```
% vcs basic.v -sverilog +optconfigfile+basic_cfg -partcomp -hsopt=hsimsdfic % simv VCS creates two new partitions dut_1 and dut_2 .
```

## Limitations

The feature has the following limitations:

- The feature only works for manual partitioning with cross-partition INTERCONNECT delays in top partition.
- The feature only works for INTERCONNECT delays on partition boundaries.
- Cross-partition SDF for mixed HDL design is not supported.
- Instance instantiation inside a generate block is not supported.
- Different partitions with different timescale is not supported.
- Instance arrays are not supported.
- Extended identifiers are not supported.

## Removing Redundant Partitions in Incremental Compile Flow

During incremental elaboration, due to a change in the design, Partition Compile generates a new partition, making the old partition redundant. The -partcomp=incr\_clean option removes the redundant partition to save the disk space.

## Usage

The following is the usage of this feature:

```
vcs -sverilog -full64 test.sv -partcomp -partcomp=incr_clean +optconfigfile+test.cfg
```

## Example

## Consider the following test cases:

```
//top.sv module top; reg r = 1'b0; reg r1 = 1'b0; initial forever #5 r = !r; initial #100 $finish; mid #(7) m1(r); mid #(8) m2(r); mid #(9) m3(r); always @* $display("Hello12345678", $time, r, top.m1.r_mid); endmodule //top1.sv module top; reg r = 1'b0; reg r1 = 1'b0; initial forever #5 r = !r; initial #100 $finish; mid #(1) m1(r); mid #(2) m2(r); mid #(3) m3(r); always @* $display("Hello12345678", $time, r, top.m1.r_mid); endmodule //mid.sv module mid (input reg w); parameter P = 8; reg r_mid; assign r_mid = w; genvar i; for(i =0 ; ibot b2(); always @* $display($time, $time, r_mid, w); endmodule //bot.sv
```

<!-- image -->

## Chapter 9: Compile Time Productivity

```
Partition Compile module bot (); reg r_bot; endmodule
```

The following is the test.cfg configuration file used in this feature:

```
//test.cfg partition cell top; partition cell mid; partition cell bot;
```

## Run the following commands without this feature:

```
vcs -sverilog -full64 top.sv mid.sv bot.sv -partcomp +optconfigfile+test.cfg vcs -sverilog -full64 top1.sv mid.sv bot.sv -partcomp +optconfigfile+test.cfg
```

## Output:

The new partitions are generated for mid module in partitionlib/ directory, and the old partitions are retained.

```
% ls partitionlib/ bot_dObXyd/ mid_1qIW3/ mid_IJ7J4b/ mid_Vp2Eg/ top_ztS8Pb/ DEFAULT/ mid_HGbGLc/ mid_qZSFPc/ mid_VqNBDd/ _vcs_pc_package__q2MOFc/
```

Run the following commands with this feature, that is, using -partcomp=incr\_clean option in both the commands:

```
vcs -sverilog -full64 top.sv mid.sv bot.sv -partcomp -partcomp=incr_clean +optconfigfile+test.cfg vcs -sverilog -full64 top1.sv mid.sv bot.sv -partcomp -partcomp=incr_clean +optconfigfile+test.cfg
```

## Output:

The redundant partitions are removed in partitionlib/ directory, that saves the disk space.

```
% ls partitionlib/ bot_dObXyd DEFAULT mid_1qIW3 mid_qZSFPc mid_VqNBDd top_ztS8Pb _vcs_pc_package__q2MOFc
```

## Rewriting XMRs to VPI Calls

VCS rewrites the XMRs to VPI calls using -partcomp=xmr\_mark\_for\_incr option. VCS provides better incremental compile time performance when DUT remains same but TB has changing XMRs from DUT.

<!-- image -->

This feature supports the following XMRs:

- XMR must be top down XMR only.
- Used in force/release statements.
- Load usage.

## Use Model

Use the following use model to enable this feature:

```
$vcs test.v -sverilog -full64 +optconfigfile+test.cfg -partcomp -partcomp=xmr_mark_for_incr
```

Rewrite occurs only for the XMRs specified in the modules in xmr\_mark\_for\_incr configuration rule.

## Configuration File

User needs to specify all the partitions and the XMRs which are changing across the compile in xmr {all\_module} configuration rule to avoid recompilation of target partitions.

Following are the configurations used for this feature:

## Example 61 test.cfg

```
// +optconfigfile configuration file partition cell mid; partition cell bdie_behav;xmr_mark_for_incr {top}; xmr_mark_for_incr {bdie_behav}; xmr {all_modules} {vec}; xmr {all_module} {vec2};
```

## Example

Following is the example of this feature:

```
module top; mid m(); bdie_behav b(); wire [7:0] TEMPERATURE_BDIE; `ifdef INCR assign TEMPERATURE_BDIE = top.m.vec2[7:0]; `else assign TEMPERATURE_BDIE = top.m.vec[7:0]; `endif always @(TEMPERATURE_BDIE) begin $display("\nvalue:%d", TEMPERATURE_BDIE); end endmodule module mid; reg [7:0] vec;
```

<!-- image -->

```
reg [7:0] vec2; endmodule module bdie_behav; initial begin force top.m.vec = 20; #20 release top.m.vec; #30 force top.m.vec = 56; #10 release top.m.vec; #100 $finish; end endmodule
```

## Limitations

The following are the limitations of this feature:

- Relative XMRs
- Bi-direct XMRs
- Non-constant RHS in force
- MDA
- Low power flow
- Partial Elaboration (PE)
- Internal modules generated from VCS
- SVA properties and sequences
- Any other driver usage than force/release
- XMRs in interface and SV code

## Partition Compile Limitations

The following are the limitations with partition compile:

- Delayed or conditional SDF annotation is not supported.
- The -race option is not supported.
- Utilities like -metadump , -Xrawtokens can be used in regular compile to generate the information.
- Dynamic Reconfiguration
- Dynamic configuration with SDF is not supported.
- Dynamic configuration with VHDL

<!-- image -->

VHDL instance inside dynamic configuration enabled module

Dynamic configuration enabled instance in VHDL

- Interface instances with reference ports inside dynamic configuration enabled module.
- XMR across PE is not supported in partition compile flow.
- XMR referrer in PE module connected as module reference port is not supported in partition compile flow.
- Cross-partition SDF (VHDL) is not supported.
- Only designs with SystemC on top are supported.
- When using VMC/SWIFT models then the VMC model cannot be a top-level module of the design.
- Verilog-AMS Mixed Signal Simulation
- Verilog-AMS amsd ie and setd commands are supported.
- GenBlock in Verilog-AMS flow is supported.
- Mixed Signal Simulation with FINESIM. (No HSIM and Nanosim compatibility with VCS).
- Partition of top-level cell in the Mixed-Signal setup file is not supported in partition compile flow.
- Multiple drivers for wreal net are not supported in partition compile flow.
- Coverage
- Constant analysis ( -cm\_noconst / -cm\_seqnoconst ) is more conservative in partition compile, so some objects which are marked "unreachable" in single compile are not marked in partcomp.
- The stop -thread &lt;thread\_no&gt; command is expected to be different in partition compile flow due to different thread ID between single compile and partition compile flow.
- For mixed designs, processing of assertion configuration file (through compile-time option -assert\_hier ) occurs at runtime in partition compile flow. This can have some impact on runtime performance or may capture assertion related errors during runtime instead of compile-time.
- Cross-partition DPI routine declaration mismatch error is generated at compile-time in single compile flow for inconsistent declarations of DPI and DPI-C. You can use the

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

- -error=noDPI-DRWIDT compile-time option to workaround this error in single compile flow.
- Partition Compile does not support the interface port when it is a multi-dimensional array.

## 10

## VCS Distributed Simulation

This chapter explains how to use VCS Distributed Simulation in this release in the following sections:

- Introduction
- Distributed Simulation Setup
- Synchronization Among Client Simvs
- Finish Behavior
- DUT Synchronization
- Testbench Phase Synchronization
- Testbench Data Transfer of Class Objects
- Debugging Distributed Simulation
- Limitations
- Quick Reference: VCS Distributed Simulation Options

## Introduction

Subsystems compile and simulate individually as separate blocks developed for multidie verification. However, integrating these subsystems in a top-level SoC poses various challenges including the resolution of modules with the same names and class/package name collision. This process needs to be repeated with every new revision of subsystems. Also, the high-memory consumption of huge designs and ever-increasing memory requirement of simulation require high-capacity machines to simulate entire designs.

VCS Distributed Simulation solution allows you to perform the following simulations:

- Homogeneous Simulation
- Heterogeneous Simulation

## Homogeneous Simulation

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

In this mode, a simulation executable (simv) is duplicated as multiple runs on the same or different machines representing multiple instances of the same module. All the data transfers across subsystems get synchronized based on the synchronization settings defined in the configuration file.

In the following figure, simv run1 and simv run2 are the same simv processes executed on two different machines.

Figure 122 Homogeneous Simulation

<!-- image -->

## Heterogeneous Simulation

In this mode, multiple simulation executables (simvs) are created for different modules with their own testbenches running on different machines in parallel. Communication across the simvs for data transfers is based on the synchronization settings defined in the configuration file.

Figure 123 Heterogeneous Simulation

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

The Distributed Simulation solution allows you to overcome synchronization issues, maintain deterministic simulation behavior during a rerun of the simulation, and achieve better runtime performance along with a reduction in memory footprint, thereby reducing the need for large-capacity machines.

## Distributed Simulation Setup

A Distributed Simulation (Distsim) setup consists of individually-developed multiple subsystems which are to be verified together. In a Distsim setup, you can run multiple subsystems on different machines, or all the subsystems on the same machine, as required.

A simv corresponding to a subsystem which is a part of a distsim setup is called a client simv . To run all the simvs in a distributed fashion using the Distsim setup, all the simvs must be compiled using the -distsim compile option, as shown in the following figure:

Figure 124 Distributed Simulation Setup

<!-- image -->

You can use the -distsim=help compile option to view all the supported -distsim options along with the purpose.

## Default Setup Using TCP/IP

You must specify the following options in the Distsim setup:

- -distsim=num\_sockets:&lt;total\_Clients&gt; : Specify the total number of clients in the setup using the -distsim=num\_sockets:&lt;total\_Clients&gt; option. The simulation can only proceed when all the clients are connected as they are mutually dependent.
- -distsim=client\_id:&lt;id&gt; : Specify the client ID using the -distsim=client\_id:&lt;id&gt; option. All the clients are distinguished based on their id to parse the configuration file.
- -distsim=server\_info:&lt;file\_path&gt; : Specify a file to dump the server information. It allows you to establish TCP connection among all the clients through a server. If the

<!-- image -->

common file system is not available to provide the server\_info file, the Distsim Flow Without Shared File System feature is used to run the Distsim flow.

- -distsim=launch\_server : To designate one of the simvs to launch the server process internally, use the -distsim=launch\_server option.

To define a specific TCP port for the server launch, refer to the User-Defined TCP Port for Server Launch feature.

To launch the server process as an independent process, refer to the Server Launch as Independent Process feature.

- -distsim=config\_file:&lt;file\_path&gt; : Specify the Distsim configuration file using the -distsim=config\_file:&lt;file\_path&gt; option. The configuration file defines connections of the DUT and testbench of simvs. To specify the configuration file with the full or relative file path with respect to the top-level connectivity file, refer to the Include Syntax in Configuration File feature.

Based on the Distsim configuration file, debug capabilities are required to be enabled during compilation. For DUT connection, you can enable force capabilities using the -debug\_acc+f compile-time option. However, for enhanced performance, refer to the Compile Time Configuration File Support section. For details on DUT, refer to the DUT Synchronization section.

For Testbench, you must add the -debug\_acc+f compile-time option. For details, refer to the Testbench Phase Synchronization and Testbench Data Transfer of Class Objects sections.

For details related to the Bidirect support and the HDL access across simvs features, refer to the Bidirect Support and HDL Access Across Simvs sections.

For information related to the synchronization of client simvs, refer to the Synchronization Among Client Simvs section.

## User-Defined TCP Port for Server Launch

All the ports in a network might not be open to establish a TCP/IP connection due to network security reasons. The User-Defined TCP Port feature passes the required port in the command line to the master simv.

## Note:

The User-Defined TCP port feature is required only for the Server, when launched separately, or for the master simv to launch the server. It is ignored for rest of the Clients.

The following is the runtime option:

-distsim=port:&lt;TCP port number&gt;

## Key Points to Note

- The configuration allows only single set of distributed simulation to run on a unique port.
- You need to provide different unique port numbers during a regression or you need to run multiple test cases simultaneously while using the -distsim=port:&lt;TCP port number&gt; option.

## Distsim Flow Without Shared File System

When the common file system is not available to provide the Server Info File, the Distsim Flow Without Shared File System feature is used to run Distsim flow. Therefore, instead of passing Server Info File in all the clients commands, you need to pass the IP address of the Server and the TCP port through the runtime arguments. The IP address can be a host name or an IPv4 address.

When the provided Server IP address is not correct, the client processes get timeout and exit. The default timeout is 60 minutes and you can use the following option to specify time in minutes:

```
-distsim=timeout:<time in minutes>
```

The following is the use model:

```
-distsim=ip:<ip_address> -distsim=port:<port_number>
```

## Where,

- &lt;ip\_address&gt; is the IPv4 address or the host name.
- &lt;port\_number&gt; is the TCP port number.

Using the -distsim=ip:&lt;ip\_address&gt; and -distsim=port:&lt;port\_number&gt; options, you can establish connection between the client simvs and the server or the server process.

## Examples

In the following examples, instead of using the server\_info runtime argument, the -distsim=ip:&lt;&gt; option is used to pass the IP address of the server and -distsim=port:&lt;&gt; option is used to pass the TCP port:

- Launching the server using -distsim=launch\_server

```
mkdir S0; cd S0 vcs ../w0.v -sverilog -full64 -distsim -distsim=client_id:0 -distsim=config_file:../mapping.txt -o simv0 -Mdir=csrc0 |& tee vcs.log.distsim.0 & ; cd .. mkdir S1; cd S1
```

<!-- image -->

- ·

<!-- image -->

```
vcs ../w1.v -sverilog -full64 -distsim -distsim=client_id:1 -distsim=config_file:../mapping.txt -o simv1 -Mdir=csrc1 |& tee vcs.log.distsim.1 & cd .. wait cd S0 ./simv0 -distsim=client_id:0,num_sockets:2,config_file:../mapping.txt -distsi m=port:8080 -distsim=ip:10.192.194.52 -distsim=launch_server -l sim0.log > client.log.0 & cd .. cd S1 ./simv1 -distsim=client_id:1,num_sockets:2,config_file:../mapping.txt -distsi m=port:8080 -distsim=ip:127.0.0.1 -l sim1.log > client.log.1 & cd .. Launching the server manually mkdir S0; cd S0 vcs ../w0.v -sverilog -full64 -distsim -distsim=client_id:0 -distsim=config_file:../mapping.txt -o simv0 -Mdir=csrc0 |& tee vcs.log.distsim.0 & ; cd .. mkdir S1; cd S1 vcs ../w1.v -sverilog -full64 -distsim -distsim=client_id:1 -distsim=config_file:../mapping.txt -o simv1 -Mdir=csrc1 |& tee vcs.log.distsim.1 &; cd .. wait cd S0 $VCS_HOME/bin/simv.distsim -full64 -distsim=num_sockets:2 -distsim=config_file:../mapping.txt -distsim=port:8080 -distsim=ip:localhost > server.log & ./simv0 -distsim=client_id:0 -distsim=num_sockets:2 -distsim=config_file:../mapping.txt -distsim=port:8080 -distsim=ip:localhost -l sim0.log > client.log.0 &; cd .. cd S1 ./simv1 -distsim=client_id:1 -distsim=num_sockets:2 -distsim=config_file:../mapping.txt -distsim=port:8080 -distsim=ip:localhost -l sim1.log > client.log.1 &; cd .. In the above example, localhost is the local computer with the loop back address, 127.0.0.1. You can get the IPv4 address or hostname using the following unix command: hostname -i
```

## Server Launch as Independent Process

The Server Launch as Independent Process feature allows you to run the Distsim server process as a standalone, independent process rather than having one of the client simvs launch it. This approach is useful when you want to explicitly control the server process or run it on a specific host.

<!-- image -->

You can launch the server process as an independent process using the following three points:

## · No -distsim=launch\_server Clients

None of the client simvs should use the -distsim=launch\_server option. This ensures that the server process is not launched by any of the clients.

## · Server Process Executable

The server process is launched using the executable located at $VCS\_HOME/bin/ simv.distsim . This is a dedicated executable for running the Distsim server.

## · Passing Runtime Flags

The server process must have all the -distsim runtime options that are passed to Client 0 if it is launching the server. These options include configuration details such as the number of sockets, configuration file, and server information.

You can use this feature to ensure that the server process is independent of all the client simvs and provides a known and stable server endpoint for all clients to connect to.

## For example,

```
$VCS_HOME/bin/simv.distsim -distsim=num_sockets:3,config_file:../mapping,server_info:../server.txt > ../server.log & simv0 -distsim=client_id:0,num_sockets:3,config_file:../mapping,server_info: ../server.txt  -l ../sim.log0 > ../client.log0 & simv1 -distsim=client_id:1,num_sockets:3,config_file:../mapping,server_info: ../server.txt  -l ../sim.log1 > ../client.log1 & simv2 -distsim=client_id:2,num_sockets:3,config_file:../mapping,server_info: ../server.txt  -l ../sim.log2 > ../client.log2 &
```

## Include Syntax in Configuration File

The Include Syntax in Configuration File feature enables a top level connectivity file to include lower level connectivity file. The top level connectivity file is passed with the following option: -distsim=config\_file:&lt;top level connectivity file&gt;

## Configuration File Syntax

Use include or 'include identifier to specify the configuration file with the full or relative file path with respect to the top level connectivity file. You must use double quotation marks to specify the configuration file.

## For example,

```
-distsim=config_file:top.connectivity.txt > cat top.connectivity.txt include "sub1.connectivity.txt" //RTL connections ... > cat sub1.connectivity.txt //RTL connections include "sub2.connectivity.txt" and so on...
```

## Synchronization Among Client Simvs

Synchronization is a process of communicating with multiple client simvs based on any design signal or a periodic interval. The simulation time when the client simvs initiate twoway communication with the server process to exchange the required data with other clients is called the synchronization point or sync point. Once all the clients reach their sync point, the server provides the required data and all the simvs waiting at the sync point continue.

You can synchronize client simvs using the following methods:

- Master-Sync Signal or Interval
- Multiple Synchronization Signals Using Multiple Groups

## Master-Sync Signal or Interval

A master-sync signal or interval can be used to determine the sync point for the client simv. A master-sync signal is a design signal for the simv and synchronization is triggered each time the master\_sync\_signal changes its state.

A master-sync interval is the time period specified by the user, and the synchronization is triggered periodically at the time interval defined by master\_sync\_interval .

It is mandatory to provide either a synchronization signal with master\_sync\_signal or a time interval with master\_sync\_interval as follows:

- Sync Signal Specification

The following is the syntax:

```
<master_sync_signal>: s<Client ID>: <Edge Identifier> <Hierarchical Path of Sync Signal>
```

<!-- image -->

## Where,

```
<master_sync_signal> : A required field. s<Client ID> : Optional field. Specifies client-specific synchronization signal. <Edge Identifier> : Optional field. Use posedge / negedge .
```

- Time Interval-Based Synchronization

The following is the syntax:

```
<master_sync_interval>: s<Client ID>: <interval><time unit>
```

## Where,

master\_sync\_interval : A required field.

s&lt;Client ID&gt; : Optional field. Specifies client-specific time interval.

&lt;interval&gt; : Specifies numeric time period in positive integers only.

&lt;time unit&gt; : Optional field. If not provided, the timescale of the design is used; otherwise, you can use s/ms/us/ns/ps/fs .

## Example

Consider the following example with two simulation clients, client 0 and client 1:

```
master_sync_signal:s0: top.clk[0] master_sync_signal:s1: top.clk[0]
```

## Where,

- s0 and s1 refer to the simulation clients, client 0 and client 1.
- top.clk[0] is the hierarchical path to the clock signal to be used as the master-sync signal.

This means that s0 and s1 get synchronized at every edge of top.clk[0] .

To understand how a master-sync signal is used to synchronize DUT, refer to the DUT Synchronization section.

## Multiple Synchronization Signals Using Multiple Groups

To create a distributed simulation setup, the default use model identifies a master-sync signal or master-sync interval. This master-sync signal or master-sync interval is used as the primary synchronization mechanism across multiple simvs. However, it introduces an additional complexity of adding a common clock or common time interval and managing the synchronization points. Furthermore, it impacts the performance when you need to synchronize the slower RTL connections with the faster master-sync signal or interval.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

The Multiple-Synchronization Groups feature is introduced to synchronize simulations with multiple clock domains, instead of using one master-sync signal or master-sync interval. It allows grouping signals in a synchronization group based on different clocks of a client.

A synchronization group is a group that contains a set of synchronization signals and their corresponding RTL connections. It is recognized by a group ID, which is a unique positive integer assigned to each synchronization group. A distributed simulation configuration file can contain multiple synchronization groups with unique group IDs for easy identification.

## Use Model

To enable the Multiple-Synchronization Groups feature, you must define synchronization groups with appropriate synchronization signals in the distributed simulation configuration file and run the following option:

```
-distsim=syncgrp
```

To define sync groups in the distributed simulation configuration file, use the following use model:

```
//Sync group with <group ID> sync_group:<group_id> sync_signal:s0:<Sync Signal 0> sync_signal:s1:<Sync Signal 1> sync_signal:s2:<Sync Signal 2> s0:<hier_path.signal0> = s1:<hier_path.signal1>
```

## Example

Consider the following example:

```
sync_group:0 sync_signal:s0:negedge top0.clk sync_signal:s1:negedge top1.clk sync_signal:s2:negedge top2.clk s0:top0.a1 = s1:top1.a1 s0:top0.b2 = s2:top2.b2 s1:top1.a3 = s0:top0.b3 s2:top2.a4 = s1:top1.b4 tbtrans=CH0:s0::CH1:s1 sync_group:1 sync_signal:s0:negedge top0.clk2 sync_signal:s2:negedge top2.clk2 s0:top0.a2 = s2:top2.a2 sync_group:2 sync_signal:s0:negedge top0.clk4
```

```
sync_signal:s1:negedge top1.clk4 s0:top0.b1 = s1:top1.b1
```

You must define synchronization groups in the distributed simulation configuration file using the following guidelines:

- You must use the sync\_group identifier to define the set of synchronization signals or intervals for the required clients. In the example, s0 , s1 , and s2 indicate synchronization signals for client 0, client 1, and client 2, respectively.
- You must specify RTL connections corresponding to the synchronization group. The RTL connections use synchronization of the respective synchronization group. In the example, sync\_group:0 has three clients, s0 , s1 , and s2 . When top0.clk changes in s0 , top1.clk changes in s1 , and top2.clk changes in s2 , the sync group ( sync\_group:0 ) synchronizes, and all the three simvs exchange data. However, sync\_group:1 has two clients, s0 and s2 . When top0.clk2 changes in s0 and top2.clk2 changes in s2 , the synchronization group ( sync\_group:1 ) synchronizes, and the two simvs exchange data.
- The Testbench Phase Synchronization, Testbench Data Transfer, HDL, and Save Restore features are not part of the sync groups, and the synchronization between the simvs happen at the change of the nearest synchronization signal of any of the synchronization groups. For example, s0 has top0.clk , top0.clk2 , and top2.clk4 in sync\_group:0 , sync\_group:1 , and sync\_group:2 , respectively. The testbench data for the CH0 channel ( tbtrans=CH0:s0::CH1:s1 ) is sent whenever any of the three clocks changes first.
- You can have multiple sync\_groups indicating groups of multiple synchronization signals. You can group a few clients or all the clients in a group.

## Limitations

The Multiple-Synchronization Group feature has the following limitations:

- Bidirect connections are not supported.
- The synchronization interval and the secondary synchronization signal are not supported.

<!-- image -->

## Finish Behavior

The finish behavior in VCS Distsim controls how the simulation ends across all the client simvs. It determines what happens when one or more clients reach the end of their simulation and call for $finish . Distsim supports the following finish behaviors:

- Safe finish : By default, VCS waits for all the clients to finish their simulation. The simulation ends only when every client reached its own end-of-simulation point, or when an error exit happens. When an error exit happens, all the client simvs exit with an error.
- Finish order : With the -distsim=finish:first option, the simulation ends for all the clients as soon as any one client finishes. When a client finishes, the rest of the clients exit their simulation at the next synchronization point instead of continuing till the end of their simulation.

## For example,

```
simv -distsim=client_id:0,num_sockets:2,config_file:../mapping,server_info :../server.txt -distsim=finish:first
```

- Early finish : When a client finishes early, the -distsim=finish:freeze option allows you to freeze the RTL signals to their last forced values in the remaining clients. This prevents local drivers from taking over those signals after the original driver has finished.

This option is used when a client finishes early, and you want to freeze the RTL signals (that were being driven by the finished client) to their last forced values in the remaining clients. This prevents local drivers from taking over those signals after the original driver has finished.

## For example,

```
vcs test.v -sverilog -full64 -distsim -distsim=config_file:mapping.txt -o simv vcs test.v -sverilog -full64 -distsim -distsim=config_file:mapping.txt -o simvf ./simvf -distsim=client_id:0,num_sockets:2,config_file:mapping.txt,server_inf o:server.txt -distsim=launch_server -l sim0.log -distsim=finish:freeze ./simv -distsim=client_id:1,num_sockets:2,config_file:mapping.txt,server_inf o:server.txt -l sim1.log &
```

<!-- image -->

## DUT Synchronization

DUT synchronization in Distsim is a process of ensuring that the Design Under Test (DUT) instances running in different clients simvs operate in a coordinated and timealigned manner. DUT synchronization involves specifying the DUT signals that need to be connected between client simvs. At each synchronization point, the values of these DUT signals are transmitted to the appropriate client simvs.

This section consists of the following topics:

- DUT Connections
- Sample Drive Signals for DUT Connection
- DUT Connection with Constant Loads
- Bidirect Support
- Compile Time Configuration File Support
- HDL Access Across Simvs

## DUT Connections

DUT connections establish seamless communication between signals in different client simv processes. Specifically, a signal from one simv, referred to as the driver signal, can be driven by a corresponding load signal in another simv. The default behavior ensures synchronized operation. That is, the values of driver signals are sampled at designated sync points, transmitted to the other simv at the same point, and subsequently driven in the target simv at the sync point. For details on sync point, refer to the Synchronization Among Client Simvs section.

For DUT connection, synchronization between signals is specified in the Distsim configuration file at runtime.

## Use Model

Configuration file : The following is the configuration file syntax for DUT connection:

s&lt;Destination Client ID&gt;:&lt;Hierarchical Path of Driver Signal&gt; = s&lt;source Client ID&gt;:&lt;Hierarchical Path of Load Signal&gt;

## Where,

- s&lt;Destination Client ID&gt; : Specifies the client ID of the simv driven by the value.
- &lt;Hierarchical Path of Driver Signal&gt; : Specifies the full path of the driver signal in the destination client.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

- s&lt;source Client ID&gt; : Specifies the client ID of the simv that provides the value.
- &lt;Hierarchical Path of Load Signal&gt; : Specifies the full path of the load signal in the source client.

Compile time : The load signal requires read capability and the driver signal requires force capability. You can enable debug-read capability in the load signal using -debug\_access +r and debug-force capability in the driver signal using -debug\_access+f . For enhanced runtime performance, apply only selective capabilities instead of using the debug\_access options. For details on applying selective capabilities, refer to the Compile Time Configuration File Support section.

The use model of the -debug\_access+f compile-time option is as follows:

```
vcs -distsim -distsim=config_file:<config_file_name> -debug_access+f and
```

Runtime : For simulation, no extra option is required.

## Example

The following example shows a configuration file where synchronization occurs when value of the test.mid.clock\_sig signal changes:

```
master_sync_signal: test.mid.clock_sig s1:test.mid.clock_sig1 = s0:test.mid.clock_sig0 s2:test.mid.clock_sig2 = s1:test.mid.clock_sig1 s0:test.mid.clock_sig4 = s1:test.mid.clock_sig3
```

The s1:test.mid.clock\_sig1 = s0:test.mid.clock\_sig0 line indicates that the client simv with client\_id == 0 has signal test.mid.clock\_sig0 that drives test.mid.clock\_sig1 of the client simv with client\_id == 1 .

Similarly, the s2:test.mid.clock\_sig2 = s1:test.mid.clock\_sig1 line indicates that the client simv with client\_id == 1 has signal test.mid.clock\_sig1 that drives test.mid.clock\_sig2 of the client simv with client\_id == 2 .

## Note:

Scalars and vectors of the following data types are supported for the synchronization signal: reg, wire, logic, bit, enum, packed memory, interface members, packed struct members, and packed struct (using the -distsim=struct runtime option).

## Limitations

The following are the limitations of DUT connections:

- Interfaces are not supported; however, interface members of the specified data types are supported.
- The unpacked memory, real, time, memword, interface, dynamic data type, and SV data type are not supported.
- The unpacked structures are not supported.

## Sample Drive Signals for DUT Connection

The Sample Drive Signals for DUT Connection feature allows you to sample and drive at two different signals. The sample and drive signals are different from the synchronization signal. Therefore, they are used for sampling and driving the signal and not for synchronization with other client simv.

## Use Model

Compile time and Runtime : You must follow the same compile-time options used for DUT Connections.

To specify different signals for sampling and driving signals across distributed simulation, add the -distsim=drive\_secondary\_clk runtime option.

The following is the use model of the -distsim=drive\_secondary\_clk runtime option:

```
% simv -distsim=drive_secondary_clk <other_distsim_arguments> <other_runtime_arguments>
```

Configuration file : You must use the identifier, master\_sync\_signal or master\_sync\_interval , to designate the master-sync signal or master-sync interval, respectively. Specify the connections that are to be sampled or driven with respect to a different sampling and driving signal in the following format:

```
s<Destination_Client_ID>:<Driver_Signal>=s<Source_Client_ID>:<Load_Signal> (Sample:<Sample_Signal>, Drive:<Drive_Signal>)
```

Where, in the source client, &lt;Load\_Signal&gt; is sampled at the change of &lt;Sample\_Signal&gt; and transferred to the destination client when master sync signal or interval changes. In the destination client, &lt;Drive\_Signal&gt; is driven when &lt;Drive\_Signal&gt; changes after synchronization.

## Note:

The configuration file format is limited to supporting only sample and drive signals, and it does not allow for the specification of time intervals.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

For the client-specific sample signal, add s&lt;Client ID&gt;: as the prefix in the configuration file.

The following is an example for the same configuration file with multiple synchronization signals or intervals:

```
Configuration File: // Define master sync signals for each client master_sync_signal:s0: top.clk[0] master_sync_signal:s1: top.clk[0] // Specify sample and drive clocks for DUT connections s0:top.B1 = s1:top.b1.b (sample:top.clk[1], drive:top.clk[2]) s0:top.C1 = s1:top.c1.c (sample:top.clk[1]) s0:top.D1 = s1:top.d1.d (drive:top.clk[2])
```

In the example, top.b1.b is sampled on the sample clock top.clk[1] . The sampled value is driven to top.B1 when the drive clock top.clk[2] switches value, following the master-synchronization signal, top.clk[0] .

## Adding Delay in DUT Connection

You can introduce a delay in DUT connections that adds a transport delay in the driver signal. Specify the delay in the Distsim mapping file in the following way:

```
s<Destination_Client_ID>:<Driver_Signal> = #<delay> s<Source_Signal>:<Load_Signal> or s<Destination_Client_ID>:<Driver_Signal> = #<delay><timeunits> s<Source Signal>:<Load Signal>
```

The #delay supports only positive integers, with or without timescale. To enable this feature, no additional compile or runtime options are required. For example,

```
// Define master sync signals for each client master_sync_signal:s0: top.clk[0] master_sync_signal:s1: top.clk[0] // Introduce a drive delay s0:top.E1 = #5ns s1:top.e1.e
```

In the example, s0:top.E1 is driven with a delay of 5ns with respect to the last synchronization.

## DUT Connection with Constant Loads

The DUT Connection with Constant Loads feature drives any supported DUT signal using the Verilog constants. It supports hexadecimal, binary, and decimal constants.

## For example,

```
s0:top.a = 1'b1 s1:top.b = 8'hzx s2:top.c = 2'd10 s3:top.d = 25
```

## Bidirect Support

The Bidirect Support feature connects signals across different clients through the wired gates behavior. This feature requires drivers capability on the design.

## Use Model

Compile time : The Bidirect Support feature requires driver capabilities and to add drivers capability during compile time, use the -debug\_acc+drivers compile-time option or use the configuration file.

The following is the use model for the -debug\_acc+drivers compile-time option:

```
vcs -distsim -distsim=config_file:<config_file_name> -debug_acc+drivers
```

Runtime : Additional distsim switches are not required to enable it during simulation, except adding the required connections in the configuration file in the specified format.

By default, the strength of the signals is not considered for the resolution. However, to enable the resolution of signals by honoring the respective strengths assigned to them, use the -distsim=strength runtime option. The following is the use model of the -distsim=strength option:

```
simv -distsim=strength
```

Configuration file : You must add the required connections in the configuration file in the specified format. The following is the use model of the configuration file:

```
vcs -distsim -distsim=config_file:<configuration_file_name>
```

## The following is the configuration file syntax:

```
<Gate Identifier> s<Client_ID>:<Signal> <=> s<Client_ID>:<Signal> <=> s<Client_ID>:<Signal>
```

## Where,

- &lt;Gate Identifier&gt; refers to the type of logical connection (specifically, a wired OR, a wired AND, or an INOUT) used to connect signals across different simulation clients.
- &lt;Client ID&gt; refers to the unique integer identifier for each simulation process (simv).
- &lt;Signal&gt; refers to a specific variable in the design hierarchy of a client that is to be connected via a bidirectional (WOR/WAND/INOUT) connection.

<!-- image -->

## Examples

The following is an example showing Bidirect Support feature:

```
WOR s0:top.b1.c <=> s1:top.b2.c <=> s2:top.c3 WAND s1:top.a1 <=> s3:top.a3
```

## The following are the expected behaviors:

- The signals connected through gate are to be resolved based on the gate type specified in the configuration file in the server process.
- WOR: If any signal is 1, all the connections become 1.
- WAND: If any signal is 0, all the connections become 0.
- INOUT
- If both signals are the same, the output is the same signal.
- If the signals are different, the output is X.
- If one of the signals is Z, the output is the other signal.

The WOR, WAND, and INOUT gate behavior is shown in the following truth table:

|   A | B   | WOR   | WAND   | INOUT   |
|-----|-----|-------|--------|---------|
|   0 | 0   | 0     | 0      | 0       |
|   0 | 1   | 1     | 0      | X       |
|   0 | X   | X     | 0      | X       |
|   0 | Z   | X     | 0      | 0       |
|   1 | 0   | 1     | 0      | X       |
|   1 | 1   | 1     | 1      | 1       |
|   1 | X   | 1     | X      | X       |
|   1 | Z   | 1     | X      | 1       |

- The signals on the client side are forced with the resolved value sent by the server.

For example,

```
wire [1:0] a; reg [1:0] b; reg [1:0] c; reg [1:0] d;
```

<!-- image -->

```
WOR s0:top.a <=> s1:top.b <=> s2:top.c
```

The top.a signal in the Client 0, the top.b signal in Client 1, and the top.c signal in Client 2 are connected to the Bidirect WOR gate.

The values of these signals are sent to the server, where they are resolved using the WOR gate. The final resolved value is sent back to all the clients and the signals are forced with the resolved value.

## Limitations

The following are the limitations of the Bidirect Support feature:

- The feature supports only WOR and WAND gates.
- The feature supports wires and logic used as wire.
- The feature supports only scalar and full vectors.
- The Bidirect Support feature does not support registers, memories, bit select, part select, and memory word.
- Distsim does not support tran gate drivers for the Bidirect connections. VCS displays a warning message on the first occurrence of an active tran gate driver.
- The strength resolution is not supported for supply0, supply1, tri0, tri1, triand, trior, WAND, and WOR data types.

## Compile Time Configuration File Support

Using the Compile Time Configuration File Support feature for the limited debug capabilities, you can avoid adding the global debug\_access debug capabilities for distsim. Instead, you can pass the distsim configuration file at compile time which enables the required debug capabilities, such as deposit/force/release, only on the relevant connectivity signals.

## Use Model

Compile time : The following is the compile option:

```
-distsim=config_file:<Distsim_Config_File_Path>
```

-distsim=client\_id:&lt;Client ID&gt; // For Heterogeneous systems. For Homogeneous systems, you can avoid this option.

## Example

```
#!/bin/csh -fx rm -rf simv* csrc* S*
```

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

```
vcs w0.v -sverilog -full64 -o simv0 -Mdir=csrc0 -distsim -distsim=config_file:mapping.txt -distsim=client_id:0 | & tee vcs.log0 vcs w1.v -sverilog -full64 -o simv1 -Mdir=csrc1 -distsim -distsim=config_file:mapping.txt -distsim=client_id:1 | & tee vcs.log1 mkdir S0 mkdir S1 cd S0 ../simv0 -distsim=client_id:0,num_sockets:2,config_file:../mapping.txt,server_inf o:../server.txt  -l ../sim.log0 -distsim=launch_server > ../client.log0 & cd .. cd S1 ../simv1 -distsim=client_id:1,num_sockets:2, config_file:../mapping.txt,server_info:../server.txt  -l ../sim.log1 > ../client.log1 & cd ..
```

The above example is of a Heterogeneous system which consists of the distsim configuration file, (-distsim=config\_file:mapping.txt) , and the client ID, (-distsim=client\_id:0 or 1) , options to enable the required debug capabilities for the design and save runtime.

## Limitations
